lead: The bandwidth an FM wave needs grows with its modulation index β = Δf/f<sub>m</sub>. For small β, narrowband FM has a carrier and one sideband pair, like AM but with the pair turned 90° to the carrier, so an envelope detector cannot recover the tone. For large β, wideband FM spreads into many sidebands spaced f<sub>m</sub> apart, sized by Bessel functions. Carson's rule, B<sub>T</sub> ≈ 2(Δf + f<sub>m</sub>), gives the channel width to allow. Broadcast FM, two-way radio and FM links use this estimate to plan spectrum.
prereq: You need: the FM wave and the modulation index β (see Frequency and phase modulation concepts).

sections.h3: Narrowband FM: a carrier and one sideband pair

blocks.text: Take a tone-modulated FM wave s(t) = A<sub>c</sub> cos(2πf<sub>c</sub> t + β sin 2πf<sub>m</sub> t). If β is small, cos(β sin x) ≈ 1 and sin(β sin x) ≈ β sin x, so:
s(t) ≈ Ac cos 2πfc t − βAc sin 2πfm t · sin 2πfc t
A<sub>c</sub> is the carrier amplitude in V; f<sub>c</sub> the carrier and f<sub>m</sub> the tone frequency in Hz; β = Δf/f<sub>m</sub>.

Expanding the product gives a carrier plus one pair: A<sub>c</sub> cos 2πf<sub>c</sub> t + (βA<sub>c</sub>/2)[cos 2π(f<sub>c</sub> + f<sub>m</sub>)t − cos 2π(f<sub>c</sub> − f<sub>m</sub>)t]. Each sideband has amplitude βA<sub>c</sub>/2. The lower one carries a minus sign, so the pair adds up at 90° to the carrier. The envelope therefore stays close to A<sub>c</sub> and holds almost no message; the message is in the phase. (AM has the same three lines but with both sidebands positive, which is why AM moves the envelope.)

This is narrowband FM (NBFM). The bandwidth for one tone is 2fm, or 2W for a message band of width W. A working test: β ≤ 0.2, where the second sideband pair is only 5 % of the first (J2(0.2)/J1(0.2) = 0.050). Some books allow up to 0.3. NBFM is used in voice radios and as the first stage of indirect FM generation.
For larger β the small-angle steps fail and the exact expansion is needed. The wave becomes a sum of lines at f<sub>c</sub> + n f<sub>m</sub>, for every whole number n, positive and negative.
s(t) = Ac Σ Jn(β) cos 2π(fc + n fm)t

J<sub>n</sub>(β) is the Bessel function of the first kind, order n; line n sits at f<sub>c</sub> + n f<sub>m</sub> with amplitude A<sub>c</sub> |J<sub>n</sub>(β)|; lines are spaced f<sub>m</sub> apart; J<sub>−n</sub>(β) = (−1)ⁿ J<sub>n</sub>(β).

A negative J<sub>n</sub>(β) is a 180° phase reversal, not negative power; power uses J<sub>n</sub>². The carrier line is A<sub>c</sub> J<sub>0</sub>(β), which vanishes where J<sub>0</sub>(β) = 0; the first such β is 2.405, used to calibrate deviation. Because Σ J<sub>n</sub>²(β) = 1 over all n, the total power stays A<sub>c</sub>²/2 (watts in a 1 Ω load) whatever β is: modulation only moves power from the carrier to the sidebands. The table gives the values used in this chapter.

Beyond about n = β + 1 the lines fall away fast. Counting β + 1 significant pairs, each spaced f<sub>m</sub>, gives a total span of 2(β + 1)f<sub>m</sub>. This is Carson's rule; it holds about 98 % or more of the power.

B<sub>T</sub> is the transmission bandwidth in Hz; β the modulation index; f<sub>m</sub> the highest modulating frequency in Hz; Δf the peak deviation in Hz. With a message band W, β becomes the deviation ratio D = Δf/W.

For large β, B<sub>T</sub> ≈ 2Δf, the band the carrier sweeps; for small β, B<sub>T</sub> ≈ 2f<sub>m</sub>, the NBFM band. Carson's value is always 2f<sub>m</sub> above 2Δf, so 2Δf becomes a good estimate only when β is large. Broadcast FM with Δf = 75 kHz and W = 15 kHz has D = 5 and B<sub>T</sub> = 180 kHz. Some syllabi call this the transmission bandwidth of FM.

examples.question: An FM broadcast transmitter has peak deviation Δf = 75 kHz and the highest modulating tone f<sub>m</sub> = 15 kHz. Find β, the significant sideband pairs by β + 1, the Carson bandwidth and the swept band 2Δf.
steps: Check with the other form: 2(Δf + f<sub>m</sub>) = 2(75 + 15) = 180 kHz.
2Δf = 150 kHz. This is only the band the carrier sweeps; the allocation follows Carson, 180 kHz.
examples.answer: β = 5, about 6 pairs, B<sub>T</sub> = 180 kHz, 2Δf = 150 kHz.

examples.question: A 10 V carrier is frequency modulated by a 5 kHz tone with β = 2 and drives a 50 Ω load. Find the amplitude and power of the carrier and of each sideband pair up to n = 4, the fraction of power inside the Carson band, and compare β = 0.2.
steps: Total power = A<sub>c</sub>²/(2R) = 100/100 = 1 W, whatever β is.
Pair 1 (f<sub>c</sub> ± 5 kHz): 10 × 0.5767 = 5.767 V each; power of the pair 2 × 5.767²/100 = 0.665 W. Running total 0.715 W.
Pair 2 (± 10 kHz): 3.528 V; pair power 0.249 W. Total 0.964 W.
Pair 3 (± 15 kHz): 1.289 V; pair power 0.033 W. Total 0.998 W, that is 99.8 %.
Pair 4 (± 20 kHz): 0.340 V; pair power 0.0023 W. Total 0.9999 W.
Carson band = 2(2 + 1) × 5 = 30 kHz, which is pairs 1 to 3: 99.8 % of the power.
For β = 0.2: carrier 9.900 V, first pair 0.995 V (≈ βA<sub>c</sub>/2 = 1 V), second pair 0.050 V carrying only 2 × 0.05²/100 = 0.00005 W. One pair is enough: narrowband.
examples.answer: Carrier 2.239 V (0.050 W); pairs 5.767, 3.528, 1.289 and 0.340 V carrying 0.665, 0.249, 0.033 and 0.002 W; the 30 kHz Carson band holds 99.8 % of the 1 W. At β = 0.2 only one pair matters.

traps: Carson's rule is 2(β + 1)f<sub>m</sub> = 2(Δf + f<sub>m</sub>), not 2Δf and not 2βf<sub>m</sub>; those are only its large-β limit.
β = Δf/f<sub>m</sub> is dimensionless. Do not use Δf/f<sub>c</sub>: the carrier sets where the spectrum sits, not how wide it is.
NBFM and AM both show three lines, but the NBFM lower sideband is negative. An envelope detector gives almost no message from NBFM.
Sidebands are spaced f<sub>m</sub> apart, not 2f<sub>m</sub>. The pair at f<sub>c</sub> ± f<sub>m</sub> is one pair.
J<sub>n</sub>(β) can be negative. That is a 180° phase reversal; the power of a line uses J<sub>n</sub>², and the total stays A<sub>c</sub>²/2.

quiz.q: Define β for a single-tone FM wave and give its unit.
quiz.a: β = Δf/f<sub>m</sub>, the peak deviation over the tone frequency, both in Hz. It has no unit; it equals the peak phase deviation in radians.

quiz.q: Why are FM sidebands spaced by f<sub>m</sub>?
quiz.a: The excess phase β sin 2πf<sub>m</sub> t repeats every 1/f<sub>m</sub>, so the complex envelope is periodic with period 1/f<sub>m</sub>. Its Fourier series has lines at multiples of f<sub>m</sub>, which sit at f<sub>c</sub> + n f<sub>m</sub> after the carrier.

quiz.q: Why does an envelope detector fail for NBFM?
quiz.a: The sideband pair has opposite signs, so its resultant is at 90° to the carrier. To first order the envelope stays A<sub>c</sub>, so the message is not in the envelope.

quiz.q: An FM tone has Δf = 10 kHz and f<sub>m</sub> = 2 kHz. Find β, the significant pairs and the Carson bandwidth.
quiz.a: β = 10/2 = 5. Pairs ≈ 6. B<sub>T</sub> = 2(10 + 2) = 24 kHz (2Δf alone would be 20 kHz).

quiz.q: For β = 2 and f<sub>m</sub> = 5 kHz, find Δf, the Carson bandwidth and 2Δf.
quiz.a: Δf = βf<sub>m</sub> = 10 kHz. B<sub>T</sub> = 2(2 + 1) × 5 = 30 kHz. 2Δf = 20 kHz.

quiz.q: A 10 V FM wave has β = 2.405. What is the carrier line, and where has its power gone?
quiz.a: Carrier = 10 J<sub>0</sub>(2.405) ≈ 0 V: the carrier vanishes. The power, still 10²/2 = 50 W in 1 Ω, sits in the sidebands, mainly the first pair (10 × 0.5191 = 5.19 V) and the second (4.32 V).

quiz.q: Why is the Carson bandwidth 2f<sub>m</sub> wider than 2Δf, and when does the difference matter?
quiz.a: Carson is 2Δf + 2f<sub>m</sub>. The extra 2f<sub>m</sub> covers the sidebands that lie beyond the swept band, which exist because the frequency changes at rate f<sub>m</sub>. It matters when β is small: at β = 1 Carson is twice 2Δf; at β = 10 it is only 10 % more.

beyond: Not for the exam. Software-defined radios check FM spectra with an FFT, and Carson's rule is the usual first choice of filter width. Digital FM modes such as GFSK in Bluetooth face the same deviation-versus-bandwidth trade with shaped pulses. Regulators specify an occupied bandwidth (99 % of power) that is close to Carson for broadcast FM. Search for FM spectral occupancy and Bessel null deviation calibration.

figure.caption: Line spectra with A<sub>c</sub> = 10 V. For β = 0.2 there is one sideband pair and the lower line is negative, so the pair is in quadrature with the carrier; for β = 2 (worked example 2) the lines are 10 J<sub>n</sub>(2) volts, and the Carson band of three pairs holds 99.8 % of the power.
